subject: application of a time-removal model on consecutive point counts data.

messages.author: 32da4f3ddb361a0e
messages.subject: application of a time-removal model on consecutive point counts data.
parts:
Dear unmarked community,

 

I need advise on determining the type of model that would help take the most advantage of my data.

 

I conducted bird point counts in 100 sites, using circular plots of 50m and grouping birds into two distance bins (0-25m, 25-50m).

I visited each site one time. On each visit I conducted three consecutive 6 minutes point counts. Therefore, I counted bird for 18 minutes total.

 

One option I am exploring is to use a time-removal framework. However, my design technically is not time removal because in the field I counted all birds again on each point count. I did not discard a bird that I counted on time 1 during time 2. But to build the data frame for time removal, I would assume that if I have the same number of bird on each time, then they are the same individuals in both counts. 

 

Does anyone have tried this?

What could be the limitation of this approach?

 

I will appreciate your comments and advise,

Isabel

messages.author: 4a635fe980c8c1cd
messages.subject: Re: application of a time-removal model on consecutive point counts data.
parts:
Hi Isabel,

I wouldn't fit a time-removal model, for reasons that you bring up. Instead, I think that I would just use the Binomial N-mixture model (fit in unmarked with the pcount function). The data (repeated counts) more or less directly align with the likelihood of that model; that these are repeated intervals over one visit rather than repeated visits with a single interval shouldn't really matter other than changing how one might think about interpreting and modeling variation in N. For example, something like Julian Date might make more sense as a covariate for lambda here rather than a covariate for p, as it might traditionally be used. 

I guess you could theoretically fit a generalized distance sampling model, but with two bins, I'm not sure you'd be able to meaningfully estimate detection parameters.

Cheers,

John

messages.author: 32da4f3ddb361a0e
messages.subject: Re: application of a time-removal model on consecutive point counts data.
parts:
Hi, John. 
Your suggestion makes sense to me. I compared the Binomial N-mixture model and g distance sampling and the first one gives a smaller N estimates, much closer to the actual total number of counts, when compare to a g distance sampling. 

There is only on more thing that  confuses me. I have seen quite a few papers, in relatively good journals, where the authors used distance sampling models using only 2 bins.
 I wonder if anyone in the unmarked community has built distance sampling model with two bins, and if there is any procedure, like a goodness of fit test, that I could use to check the fit of the distance model.

thanks again for your comments and suggestions, 
Isa
